title: Standard and Formal English
summary: The difference between Standard and non-standard English and between formal and informal register, the features of each, formal vocabulary, and how Checkpoint asks you to identify them, with practice and answers.

blocks.text: 1. Two different ideas: standard and formal
Students often mix up these two ideas. They are not the same thing.

items: **Standard English** is about **correctness**: English that follows the accepted rules of grammar and vocabulary. It is used in exams, books, news and formal writing.
**Formal English** is about **register** (how formal or informal a text is): the level of politeness, distance and seriousness chosen for the reader and purpose.

blocks.text: A text can be **informal but still Standard**: I'm so excited about the trip! Can't wait to see you. (chatty, but no grammar errors). A sentence like We was gonna go is **non-standard** (wrong grammar for written English). In an exam, your writing must always be Standard English, and its register must match the task.

blocks.title: Key words
items: **Standard English**: English that follows the accepted rules of grammar, used in exams and formal writing.
**Non-standard English**: English that breaks those rules, common in everyday speech, dialects and text messages.
**Register**: how formal or informal a text is.
**Contraction**: two words shortened into one with an apostrophe (don't, it's, we'll).
**Colloquial / slang**: very informal, everyday spoken words (loads of, mates, cool).

rows: She did / has done her homework.
Me and Ali went to the park.
Ali and I went to the park.

blocks.text: **Why a writer uses non-standard English on purpose:** in fiction, in dialogue, to make a character sound realistic, to show the character's age, background, region or personality, to create a casual, informal voice and sometimes for humour. In your own writing, use Standard English everywhere **except** inside a character's speech.

rows: Precise, often longer words: obtain, assist, purchase
Everyday words, slang, phrasal verbs: get, help out, buy
Often third person, impersonal It is believed that...
First and second person: I, you, we
Passive is common: The decision was made...
Exclamation marks, dashes, brackets for chatty asides
Reports, formal letters, news, information texts, speeches to officials
Blogs, diaries, emails and letters to friends, some magazine articles

blocks.text: **Formality is a scale.** A letter to a head teacher is formal, a school magazine article is semi-formal (friendly but still careful), and a message to a friend is informal. Choose the level that suits your **reader** and **purpose**.

groups.title: Formal openings and requests
items: I am writing to express my concern about...
I would be grateful if you could...
I would like to suggest that...
Please do not hesitate to contact me if...

groups.title: Informal equivalents (for friendly texts only)
items: Can't wait to hear from you!

rows: I'm writing because the park isn't safe.
I am writing because the park is not safe.
Loads of kids reckon the canteen food is rubbish.
Many students believe the quality of the canteen food is poor.
Dear Sir, hope you're good! I would like to complain...
Dear Sir, I am writing to complain...
Dear Ali, I wish to inform you that I commenced my holiday.
Hi Ali, Guess what? My holiday has finally started!
We was told the trip is cancelled.
We were told that the trip had been cancelled.

blocks.text: **Question style:** Identify two features that make this text formal. Name the feature **and** quote an example for each: 1. No contractions, e.g. 'it is not possible'. 2. The passive voice, e.g. 'visitors are requested to...'.

**Worked example.** Visitors are requested to remain on the marked paths at all times. Failure to do so may result in damage to rare plant species. Two formal features: (1) passive voice, Visitors are requested. (2) Formal, precise vocabulary, Failure to do so may result in. Also (3) no contractions and no direct address to you.

You may also be asked why a character speaks in non-standard English, or why a writer uses an informal, chatty tone (for example, in a blog: to build a friendly relationship with the reader and make the text feel personal).

**In your writing**, match the register to the task: formal for letters to officials, reports, news reports and speeches to adults, informal (but still Standard English) for diaries, blogs and emails to friends. Keep the register **consistent** from the first line to the last.

blocks.title: الرسمي وغير الرسمي
items: Standard English يعني قواعد صح، و Formal يعني أسلوب رسمي. ممكن تكتب إيميل لصاحبك غير رسمي بس القواعد لازم تبقى صح.
في الخطاب الرسمي: من غير اختصارات (do not مش don't)، ومن غير كلام عامي زي gonna أو loads of.
في السؤال: اذكر الـ feature وهات مثال من النص لكل واحدة.

items.q: Rewrite in Standard English: Me and him seen the accident but we didn't say nothing.
items.a: He and I saw the accident, but we didn't say anything.

items.q: In a story, a character says: "Ain't nobody gonna stop me now!" Why has the writer used non-standard English? (1 mark)
items.a: To make the character's speech sound realistic and show their confident, casual personality (and perhaps their background).

items.q: Identify two features that make this text formal: Residents are advised that the swimming pool will be closed for maintenance. We apologise for any inconvenience caused.
items.a: Any two: passive voice (Residents are advised, will be closed). Formal vocabulary (maintenance, inconvenience). No contractions (will be, not 'll). Polite, impersonal tone (We apologise for any inconvenience caused).

items.q: Rewrite in a formal register: Hey, we're gonna need loads of help with the fair, so grab your mates and come along!
items.a: We will require a large number of volunteers for the fair. Students are invited to attend with their friends.

items.q: Is this sentence formal or informal, and is it Standard English? Honestly, the new café is amazing – you've got to try the mango cake!
items.a: Informal (contraction, Honestly, exclamation mark, direct address to you), but it **is** Standard English: the grammar is correct.

items.q: Identify two features that make this blog extract informal: So, here's the thing. I tried to bake bread last week (big mistake!) and it came out like a rock.
items.a: Any two: contractions (here's), chatty opener (So, here's the thing), brackets for a humorous aside (big mistake!), exclamation mark, first person and a casual simile (like a rock).

items.q: Replace the informal words with formal ones: We need to find out why loads of students don't get enough sleep.
items.a: We need to discover / investigate why numerous / many students do not get sufficient sleep.

items.q: Correct the non-standard forms: You should of seen it. Them birds was huge.
items.a: You should have seen it. Those birds were huge.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Standard = correct grammar (always in your writing, except in dialogue). Formal = no contractions, precise words, passive, impersonal. Match the register to the reader and keep it consistent.
